headline: Connecticut senators split with UConn over Senate college-sports overhaul
dek: The Protect College Sports Act passed 77-22 after Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy voted no, even as a Blumenthal amendment could give UConn more room to pursue a Power Four conference.
body: Connecticut’s two Democratic U.S. senators voted against a sweeping college-sports bill that cleared the Senate this week, putting them at odds with University of Connecticut officials and men’s basketball coach Dan Hurley over whether Congress should impose a national framework on athlete pay, transfers and conference competition.

The Protect College Sports Act passed 77-22 on Sept. 28, according to coverage by Connecticut Public and CT Mirror (https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-09-29/senate-passes-college-sports-bill-amid-opposition-from-ct-senators). The legislation is designed to replace a patchwork of court rulings, state laws and conference policies with federal rules. It would allow one penalty-free transfer for most athletes rather than unlimited transfers, while creating exceptions for situations such as sexual misconduct, a program closing or a head coach leaving. It also would set five years of eligibility and an age limit of 24 for players covered by the bill.

For UConn, the most immediate Connecticut-specific provision was an amendment by Sen. Richard Blumenthal that passed by voice vote. It raises from 19 to 20 the number of teams permitted in the Power Four conferences: the Big Ten, Southeastern Conference, Atlantic Coast Conference and Big 12. The change could make it easier for a school such as UConn to join one of those leagues, but it does not award the university an invitation or decide which conference would accept it.

Blumenthal still voted no. In his official statement (https://www.blumenthal.senate.gov/newsroom/press/release/blumenthal-votes-against-legislation-that-fails-to-protect-college-athletes), he said the bill’s protections would depend too heavily on NCAA enforcement and argued that the measure would preserve the dominance of the current Power Four membership. He also sought, but did not receive consideration for, amendments that would give state attorneys general enforcement authority, restrict private-equity and foreign-sovereign-wealth involvement, increase damages for violations and remove a notice-and-cure process for athlete lawsuits.

Sen. Chris Murphy’s objection focused on compensation and worker power. He argued that the bill would cap athletes’ earnings while granting the NCAA and conferences a broad antitrust exemption. WSHU reported that both Connecticut senators opposed the measure and that Murphy favored allowing college athletes to organize and bargain collectively instead (https://www.wshu.org/connecticut-news/2026-09-29/murphy-blumenthal-ncaa-college-sports-bill). Murphy said before the vote that the legislation could ultimately damage college athletics if athletes reject a system they view as limiting their pay.

The bill would set additional national standards for name, image and likeness agreements, commonly called NIL deals. The Connecticut Public and CT Mirror report said athletes would have to report compensation above $600 and agents would face a 5% fee cap. The bill also gives the NCAA and conferences an antitrust shield for enforcing the new standards, a provision supporters say is needed to make a uniform system workable and critics say could weaken athletes’ ability to challenge decisions.

UConn has said it wants Congress to act quickly because the current system makes long-term planning difficult for schools and athletes. The university has advocated a uniform framework, while Hurley said a national standard was necessary even if the legislation was imperfect. That support reflects UConn’s position as a high-profile basketball program in the Big East and a school whose conference future is part of the broader realignment debate; it does not mean the university endorsed every provision or guarantee in the Senate bill.

The next major uncertainty is the House. The measure’s bill record is available through Congress.gov (https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/4668), but the House is in recess through the November midterm elections. Senate sponsor Ted Cruz has urged House leaders to return early, while reporting by CT Mirror and Connecticut Public said that outcome is unlikely and the bill’s support in the House is unclear. Until the House passes identical legislation and it is signed, the Senate vote changes no athlete’s current eligibility, NIL arrangement or conference membership.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut Senators Oppose Senate College-Sports Bill
seoDescription: Connecticut senators Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy opposed the Protect College Sports Act even after a UConn-related conference amendment passed.
